newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia-made labels smell of race row - exporter.
newsitem.headline: Australia-made labels smell of race row - exporter.

text.p: An Australian cosmetics company said on Friday it was under pressure to remove "Australian made" labels from its exports to Asia because Australia could be seen by consumers as a racist nation.
The Body Collection Pty Ltd, which sells skin care products to retailers in five Asian countries, said some Asian clients wanted the labels removed in case shoppers shunned them.
"They are concerned the whole Australian image can be associated with the racism debate," managing director David Southwick told Reuters.
"That's all they read about, and they're concerned that by stocking Australian-made products in their stores it may actually do harm to their image and their sales," he added.
Australia has been engulfed in a bitter debate over levels of Asian immigration, a debate that has raised concerns in both business and government for Australia's Asian trade ties.
Independent legislator Pauline Hanson sparked the debate by warning in her maiden speech to parliament last year that Australia was in danger of "being swamped by Asians".
She has since formed a far-right political party, One Nation, which has drawn strong support in opinion polls.

The Body Collection said on Friday it had so far declined to remove "Australian made" labels from its products and had instead decided to spend up to A$500,000 (US$380,000) on an Asian marketing campaign.
Consumer competitions for trips to Australia will also be run as part of the campaign, it said.
"If we were to remove our 'Australian made' logos, it would do harm to our business because that's our big point of difference," Southwick said.
The logos are an official design approved for use by the government.
Southwick said the company decided to launch the Asian marketing campaign, aimed directly at shoppers, after he paid recent visits to customers in Hong Kong, Malaysia and Japan.
The firm also sells into Singapore and Thailand, he added.
"It's a concern that her (Hanson's) campaign is not slowing down, it's getting stronger and stronger and it's a concern for business," Southwick said.
